key_identity: Positive speed <=> positive entropy <=> non-trivial Poisson boundary, for a fixed finitely supported symmetric step law; invariance under changing the law is the question.
method: Use the Kaimanovich-Vershik equivalence: positive speed iff positive entropy iff non-trivial Poisson boundary, and ask which of these is generating-set invariant.
obstruction: No structural characterisation of Liouville groups.
result: The non-triviality of the Poisson boundary of a group (existence of non-constant bounded harmonic functions for some/all symmetric finitely supported non-degenerate steps) is NOT known to be independent of the step distribution in general, and positive entropy of the walk is equivalent to non-triviality of the boundary for the same step distribution, so the question is equivalent to: is boundary non-triviality invariant under change of finitely supported symmetric generating measure. For measures with the same support class one has comparison of entropies by the fundamental inequality h <= l v (entropy <= speed times growth), which shows h > 0 forces l > 0 for every generating set of exponential-growth groups but does not transfer positivity of l between generating sets. The known invariance results (lamplighters, groups with a Liouville/non-Liouville dichotomy decided by structure such as polynomial growth or non-amenability) all go through a structural characterisation of the boundary; a group-theoretic characterisation of positive speed would settle the question and is the true content. No new result; the reduction to 'boundary non-triviality is a property of the group' is recorded.

author: claude-probability-1000-continue-0907
key_identity: Non-constant harmonic h on a transitive graph: Var h(X_n) >= c n; with h = o(dist^{1/2}) and diffusive walk this contradicts, so no harmonic functions of growth o(r^{1/2}) on diffusive groups.
method: Test both directions on the known examples and locate the mechanism.
obstruction: Growth exponents between 1/2 and 1 are not reached by the second-moment martingale argument.
result: Diffusive groups: polynomial growth (virtually nilpotent) groups are diffusive and have no sublinear harmonic functions beyond constants (Kleiner/Colding-Minicozzi-type results give that harmonic functions of growth below linear are constant). Non-diffusive examples: non-amenable groups (positive speed) have bounded non-constant harmonic functions, which are sublinear; lamplighters Z_2 wr Z^d for d >= 3 have positive speed and bounded harmonic functions; Z_2 wr Z has speed of order n^{3/4}... in the exponent sense l(n) asymp n^{3/4} and non-constant harmonic functions of sublinear growth are expected (built from the lamp configuration). So the conjecture is consistent with every example I can check. A route to the 'diffusive implies no sublinear harmonic' direction: a sublinear harmonic function h gives a martingale h(X_n) with increments bounded by the local Lipschitz constant, and diffusivity plus sublinearity force Var(h(X_n)) = o(n)... which does not contradict martingale variance growing linearly unless the increments are controlled; the contradiction needs E[(h(X_{n+1}) - h(X_n))^2] bounded below, which holds for non-constant harmonic h on a transitive graph, giving Var h(X_n) >= c n, while sublinearity of h and diffusivity give E h(X_n)^2 <= o(n) only if h grows slower than sqrt(n) at distance sqrt(n), i.e. only for growth o(dist^{1/2}). So the martingale argument proves: a diffusive group has no non-constant harmonic function of growth o(dist^{1/2}); closing the gap from exponent 1/2 to 1 is the open content.

author: claude-probability-1000-continue-0907
method: Isolate the regime left open by the Gaussian-free-field proof.
obstruction: GFF route needs isoperimetric dimension > 4; Peierls needs cutset counts not implied by IP_{1+eps}.
result: The DGRSY argument uses the GFF on the graph, whose existence and level-set structure need the random walk to be transient with Green function decay controlled by the isoperimetric dimension d > 4; for isoperimetric dimension in (1,4] the GFF-based route fails (in dimension at most 2 the field is not even defined without renormalisation). For transitive graphs the missing cases are covered by structure theory (polynomial growth is virtually nilpotent, hence Z^d-like, hence p_c < 1 for d >= 2 by classical arguments), so the genuinely open case is NON-transitive bounded-degree graphs with isoperimetric dimension in (1, 4]. For those the natural tool is a Peierls-type argument, which needs at most exponentially many minimal cutsets of each size, a property IP_{1+eps} does not imply (there are graphs with IP_{1+eps} and super-exponentially many minimal cutsets, e.g. spherically symmetric trees with slowly growing degrees, where nonetheless p_c < 1 holds by the branching structure). No general argument found; the honest reduction is: for non-transitive graphs of isoperimetric dimension in (1,4], p_c < 1 needs either a cutset-count bound or a replacement for the GFF.

author: claude-probability-1000-continue-0907
key_identity: Unimodular: n edges from a finite cluster to infinity force a minimal cutset of size >= n/deg (mass transport); nonunimodular graphs break this.
method: Reduce to a slab/renormalisation statement and identify what replaces the Z^d cluster-uniqueness input.
obstruction: Amenable exponential-growth transitive graphs lack a renormalisation scheme; nonunimodular graphs lack the cutset bound.
result: On Z^d the proof (Pete 2008) uses the Grimmett-Marstrand renormalisation and the uniqueness of the infinite cluster to show that a finite cluster with n boundary edges to C_infinity must be enclosed by a closed surface of size at least n in the renormalised picture, whose cost is exponential. On a general transitive graph the two inputs are (i) a renormalisation scheme giving supercritical behaviour on coarse-grained blocks, available for polynomial growth via the CMT 2022 results and for nonamenable graphs via the Benjamini-Lyons-Peres-Schramm / Hutchcroft methods, and (ii) an isoperimetric bound turning 'n edges to the infinite cluster' into a large closed cutset, which holds when minimal cutsets separating a finite set from infinity have size at least a function of the set's boundary, true on unimodular transitive graphs by mass transport (a finite set with boundary n has a minimal cutset of size at least n/deg). The remaining gap is the nonunimodular case, where (ii) fails as stated (nonunimodular graphs can have finite sets with large boundary and small cutsets via heavy vertices), which is presumably why the source hedges 'unimodular?'. Rigorous partial: on unimodular transitive graphs the reduction to a renormalisation statement goes through; the renormalisation is available for polynomial growth and for nonamenable graphs; the amenable exponential-growth (e.g. lamplighter) case is the open one.

author: claude-probability-1000-continue-0907
method: Try the natural Folner sequence of balls and see what fails; then a subsequence argument.
obstruction: Interior coarse connectivity of Folner sets on amenable exponential-growth graphs.
result: For balls in Z^d the statement is a theorem (uniqueness of the giant in boxes, Grimmett-Marstrand plus the finite-box uniqueness results of Pisztora); the difficulty on a general amenable transitive graph is that a Folner set can have a thin boundary but a disconnected interior structure in which C_infinity intersect F_n splits into several macroscopic pieces linked only outside F_n. A sufficient condition is a 'coarse connectivity' of F_n: every two macroscopic sub-blocks of F_n are joined inside F_n by a path of blocks each of which contains the giant with high probability; on Z^d this is the block renormalisation, and on a general amenable graph the existence of such a Folner sequence would follow from a renormalisation as in C0143, which is available for polynomial growth. So Question 12.34 is implied, for polynomial growth, by the CMT-type supercritical sharpness plus the standard finite-box uniqueness argument (not verified in detail), and is open for amenable graphs of exponential growth, where the Folner sets are exponentially large relative to their boundary and the interior connectivity of the cluster restricted to them is uncontrolled. Reduction recorded; no proof.

author: claude-probability-1000-continue-0907
method: Compare with the Antal-Peres chemical distance theorem on Z^d and identify the input that p > p_u provides on nonamenable graphs.
obstruction: Dependence of connection events along a geodesic; no renormalisation on nonamenable graphs.
result: On Z^d for p > p_c the chemical distance is linear with exponential tails (Antal-Peres), by renormalisation. On a nonamenable transitive graph above p_u the infinite cluster is unique and 'robust' in the sense that connections between far points exist with probability bounded below (the Lyons-Schramm characterisation inf P(x <-> y) > 0), which gives finiteness of the conditional expectation of the ratio only if one can build a chemical path of length comparable to the graph distance from these connection events, i.e. a chain of overlapping connections along a geodesic; each link is an event of probability bounded below but not close to one, and the conditional expectation of the ratio requires the links to be found within a bounded number of trials, which the uniform connection bound gives with geometric tails along the geodesic PROVIDED the connection events for different links are approximately independent, which they are not (they share the same cluster). This is the same dependence problem that the Z^d proof handles by renormalisation; on nonamenable graphs no renormalisation is available, but the uniform connection probability is a strong substitute that I could not turn into a linear chemical distance without independence. The exponent kappa < 1 near p_u is a near-critical statement beyond any current tool.

author: claude-probability-1000-continue-0907
method: Check whether monotonicity in p of the FK(p,q) measures holds at all for q < 1, which the coupling needs.
obstruction: Monotonicity in p itself is unverified for q < 1; a small-graph symbolic test is the next step.
result: For q >= 1 the measures are FKG and increasing in p (Holley), which is why a monotone coupling exists; for q < 1 FKG fails and monotonicity in p is not known in general. A necessary condition: FK(p,q) must stochastically dominate FK(p',q) for p > p', i.e. every increasing event must have nondecreasing probability in p. For the single-edge marginal this holds: the probability that a fixed edge is open is p times a ratio of partition functions with the edge contracted versus deleted, and the ratio is... its p-derivative involves the covariance of the edge with the total edge count, which is positive when q >= 1 and of unknown sign for q < 1; on a single cycle one can compute exactly that the edge marginal is increasing in p for all q > 0 (the weights are w^{|omega|} q^{k(omega)} and on a cycle the cluster count is 1 if all edges open and n - |omega| otherwise, giving a marginal that is a ratio of polynomials in w with positive coefficients whose derivative is positive by a direct check I did not carry out symbolically). So the first non-trivial test is the theta graph or K_4 with q in (0,1): compute the two-edge increasing events' probabilities as functions of p and check monotonicity; a failure would answer the question negatively. Not computed in this batch; recorded as the concrete next computation together with C0091's cycle test.

author: claude-probability-1000-continue-0907
method: Test the bootstrap-percolation comparison that gives the high-dimensional limit and see why it fails at fixed d.
obstruction: Stable finite minus configurations at any density under deterministic tie rules; no monotone comparison at fixed d.
result: Morris's proof of lim p_fix(Z^d) = 1/2 compares majority dynamics with an r-neighbour bootstrap process whose critical density tends to 1/2 as d grows; at fixed d the comparison loses a constant because the minus phase can stabilise in finite blocks (a 2x2 block of minus in Z^2 is stable under majority with ties broken against flipping, and a large minus region with flat boundary is stable), so at any density below 1/2 + eps there are stable minus regions at all scales with positive density unless the plus phase erodes them, which needs the plus phase to have a percolating 'majority backbone'. On Z^2 the conjecture p_fix = 1/2 is open even though minus blocks of density just below 1/2 look subcritical, because stability of minus regions is a local (finite) property and does not require percolation. A concrete obstruction: on Z^2 with density p > 1/2 of plus, the minus phase contains, with positive density, 2x2 blocks completely surrounded by... no, a 2x2 minus block surrounded by plus flips (each minus vertex has 2 minus and 2 plus neighbours, a tie); with the tie rule 'stay', 2x2 minus blocks are stable at any density, so p_fix(Z^2) < 1 requires the tie rule to flip or the dynamics to be asynchronous with random tie-breaking; the notes presumably use the random-tie version. Under random tie-breaking the block dissolves; then the question is whether plus, once a majority, wins with probability one, and the difficulty is purely the absence of a monotone comparison at fixed d. No result.

author: claude-probability-1000-continue-0907
method: Compare unlabelled local weak limits with the labelled (Cayley diagram) version where the answer is yes.
obstruction: Recovering labels from unlabelled approximants when the Cayley graph has many automorphisms.
result: For labelled Cayley diagrams, approximability by finite labelled digraphs is soficity, and changing the generating set preserves it (relabel words). For unlabelled graphs, a finite graph sequence converging locally to the Cayley graph of one generating set need not carry labels; the question is whether one can recover a compatible labelling on most of the finite graphs. For Cayley graphs with trivial local automorphism structure (the ball of radius r has no non-trivial automorphisms fixing the centre for r large) the labelling is determined locally and (a) follows; for graphs with rich local symmetry (e.g. Cayley graphs of Z^d with standard generators have local automorphisms, but those come from the group itself and the labelling can be chosen consistently on most vertices) the recovery is a rigidity question. Rigorous partial: if the Cayley graph is 'locally rigid' in the sense that the group is the full automorphism group and the ball of radius r determines the label pattern, then unlabelled local approximability of that Cayley graph gives labelled approximability, hence soficity, hence (b) for that group and (a) for all its generating sets. The gap is Cayley graphs with large automorphism groups, e.g. free groups (the tree has a huge automorphism group and unlabelled approximants of the tree, large-girth graphs, are all fine, yet soficity of free groups is trivial), so the question is subtle exactly for non-rigid Cayley graphs of non-obviously-sofic groups. No result.

author: claude-probability-1000-continue-0907
method: Relate to the spectral characterisation of property T and to the known fact that approximants of T groups have a spectral gap in the limit.
obstruction: Spectral-gap-in-the-limit does not localise to a removable vertex set for general graphs.
result: Property T gives a uniform spectral gap for every unitary representation without invariant vectors; for finite quotients this is the classical fact that quotients of T groups form expanders. Benjamini-Schramm approximants are not quotients: they only agree locally. The known partial result is that local convergence of G_n to a T group forces the limiting spectral measure of the Laplacian to have a gap at 0, i.e. the number of eigenvalues near 0 is o(|V(G_n)|), which is exactly the statement that after removing o(n) 'bad mass' the graphs expand in an L^2 sense but not the combinatorial essential-expander statement, because small eigenvalues can come from a small number of poorly connected pieces that are not removable by deleting eps n vertices (a long path attached to an expander gives one small eigenvalue per unit of path length, removable, but a dense set of small bottlenecks is not). The conjecture is thus equivalent to converting 'o(n) eigenvalues below c' into 'eps n vertices whose removal leaves c-expanders', a Cheeger-type localisation that is false for general graphs but might hold for graphs locally resembling a T Cayley graph. No proof.

author: claude-probability-1000-continue-0907
key_identity: Atom of sigma_{e,e} at lambda => p_{2n}(e,e) >= c lambda^{2n}... does not tend to zero for |lambda| = 1; infinite groups have p_{2n}(e,e) -> 0, so the Markov operator has no atoms at +-1; atoms elsewhere are excluded by the same decay only for the extremal spectrum.
method: Record the probabilistic content (no atoms in the return-probability spectral measure) and what the known positive cases use.
obstruction: General group-algebra elements have no positivity; the problem is algebraic.
result: The random-walk form: the spectral measure of the Markov operator at the identity has no atoms iff the return probabilities p_{2n}(e,e) have no periodic component of positive mass... precisely, an atom at lambda contributes lambda^{n} to p_n(e,e) without decay, so no atoms is implied by p_n(e,e) -> 0, which holds for every infinite group (the walk is not positive recurrent). So the 'no atoms' statement for the Markov operator is immediate for infinite groups: atoms of the spectral measure sigma_{x,x} at the identity would give p_{2n}(e,e) not tending to 0. The conjecture's content is therefore for general elements of the group algebra (and matrices), where the analogous 'return probability' has no positivity and the argument fails; e.g. a = 1 - M with M the Markov operator has kernel equal to the invariant vectors, trivial for infinite groups, but for general a with mixed signs the kernel can be non-trivial in principle. Known positive cases (free groups, elementary amenable torsion-free, right-orderable groups via Linnell, torsion-free groups satisfying the Baum-Connes conjecture in the form of Kaplansky's zero-divisor conjecture) all use algebra. Partial rigorous remark recorded: the Markov-operator case is trivial by transience-type decay; the conjecture is about non-positive elements.

author: claude-probability-1000-continue-0907
independent_check: Both results are widely cited; not re-fetched in this session.
key_identity: Random d-regular max independent density 2 log d/d vs factor-of-iid bound log d/d (Rahman-Virag): the conjectured equality fails at the maximum.
method: Compare the two sets on what is known: the maximum independent set density versus the best factor-of-iid density.
obstruction: none for the refutation; the residual question is trivial by dilution
result: One inclusion is a theorem: any factor-of-i.i.d. independent set on the tree can be transferred to random d-regular graphs (large girth) with the same density up to o(1), so factor densities are achievable. The conjecture is the converse: every achievable density is a factor density. It is known to FAIL at the maximum: for large d the maximum independent set density of random d-regular graphs is 2 log d/d (1+o(1)) (Ding-Sly-Sun for large d) while factor-of-i.i.d. independent sets have density at most log d/d (1+o(1)) (Rahman-Virag 2017), a factor of 2 gap. Hence the conjecture as stated in the source is false for the maximal density, at least for large d; the surviving question is the characterisation of the achievable set below the factor threshold (which is an interval [0, alpha_factor] by dilution, already covered) versus the interval [0, alpha_max] of achievable densities. Recorded as refuted at the top density by Rahman-Virag together with Ding-Sly-Sun (bounded recall of both).

author: claude-probability-1000-continue-0907
method: Test on the two extremes: amenable limits (Ornstein-Weiss) and large-girth sequences with a tree limit.
obstruction: Entropy of a factor is not a local statistic; local-global convergence is the natural extra hypothesis.
result: For a sequence converging to an amenable transitive graph the normalised entropy of a factor converges to the Ornstein-Weiss entropy of the limiting factor process (entropy is a local-averaging quantity when Folner sets approximate). For large-girth d-regular graphs converging to the tree, two different sequences (random regular graphs versus explicit large-girth expanders) can carry the same factor F but the normalised entropy of F(G_n, omega_n) counts the number of typical configurations on G_n, which depends on global structure through the number of solutions of local constraints: this is exactly the phenomenon behind the independent-set density gap in C0151 (random regular graphs admit more independent sets than factor constructions produce). However the conjecture concerns h of the FACTOR process only, i.e. the entropy of the pushforward of the i.i.d. measure, which is determined by local statistics of F plus global correlations of the factor; Backhausz-Szegedy's work on typical processes suggests convergence holds for sequences with the 'local-global' property (random regular graphs) and may fail otherwise. A candidate counterexample: two sequences with the same local limit, one with many short cycles arranged globally and one random, and a factor whose output entropy is sensitive to global cycle structure; I could not construct the factor. No result.

author: claude-probability-1000-continue-0907
key_identity: Finite-graph complement of a ball connected in the percolation configuration <=> wired boundary condition in the limit.
method: Separate the random-cluster question from its spin-model consequence.
obstruction: Giant uniqueness for non-transitive local approximants.
result: For q = 2 the Montanari-Mossel-Sly result is about the ISING local limit on regular trees, which is the symmetric mixture of the plus and minus extremal measures; in random-cluster language this corresponds to the wired measure (the mixture of the two spin phases is the Edwards-Sokal image of the wired FK measure). So the q = 2, tree case is consistent with the question. For general q > 1 and a general nonamenable limit, a route: the finite-volume random-cluster measure on G_n is sandwiched (for q >= 1) between free and wired measures on any finite ball by monotonicity, and the local limit is sandwiched between the free and wired limits on G; the question is whether the limit hits the wired end. Wired is favoured because finite graphs have no 'boundary' (a ball's complement in G_n is connected and large), which acts like wired boundary conditions provided the complement percolates, i.e. for p above the threshold where the free and wired measures differ the finite graph's complement of a ball is itself supercritical and connected, wiring the boundary. For p below that threshold free = wired and the question is empty. So for q >= 1 the answer is yes whenever the complement of a ball in G_n is connected within the percolation configuration with high probability, which is a uniqueness-of-the-giant statement on G_n (C0141-type, proved for transitive G_n by Easo-Hutchcroft); for non-transitive G_n it is exactly the open part. Reduction: for transitive G_n and q >= 1 the answer should be yes via giant uniqueness; general G_n open.

author: claude-probability-1000-continue-0907
method: Record why the probabilistic criteria are inconclusive.
obstruction: No computable amenability criterion applies to F.
result: Positive speed of a symmetric finitely supported walk does not decide amenability (amenable groups such as lamplighters have positive speed), and the Kesten criterion (spectral radius < 1 iff nonamenable) would decide it but the spectral radius of F is not computable by current methods; numerical estimates of return probabilities on F (Haagerup-Haagerup-Ramirez-Solano) are consistent with both. Probabilistic content available: F has exponential growth and contains no free subgroup (Brin-Squier), so the Tits alternative route is closed; F is not elementary amenable; F's Folner sets, if they exist, must be exotic (Moore's lower bound on Folner function growth). No probabilistic attack recorded beyond these facts.

author: claude-probability-1000-continue-0907
key_identity: Somewhere along Z, windows of n consecutive gaps have arbitrarily small total, so no monotone map has bounded multiplicative distortion; a quasi-isometry must be a non-monotone matching.
method: Construct an explicit bijection with bounded distortion using the law of the iterated logarithm.
obstruction: Existence of a bounded-distortion non-monotone matching between two independent Poisson processes is unresolved.
result: Order both processes as ...< x_{-1} < x_0 < x_1 < ... and ...< y_{-1} < y_0 < y_1 < ... and map x_i -> y_i. Distortion: |y_i - y_j| versus |x_i - x_j| for i < j are both sums of j - i i.i.d. exponentials, so their ratio is close to 1 for large j - i by the law of large numbers, but a quasi-isometry needs a UNIFORM bound C such that |x_i - x_j|/C - c <= |y_i - y_j| <= C|x_i - x_j| + c for ALL pairs; for nearby pairs (j - i small) the ratio of two independent Gamma(k) variables is unbounded over infinitely many pairs (there are a.s. pairs with x-gap tiny and y-gap of order 1), so the index map fails. A quasi-isometry may send x_i to y_{sigma(i)} for a non-monotone sigma, but any quasi-isometry of R-like spaces is at bounded distance from a monotone one, and the additive constant c absorbs bounded gaps: with c >= 1 the small-gap problem disappears for gaps below 1, and the issue becomes long runs of small gaps in one process against long runs of large gaps in the other, i.e. whether for every n the partial sums S_n(x) and S_n(y) of the gaps satisfy S_n(y) <= C S_n(x) + c uniformly in n and in the starting index. By the LIL both partial sums are n + O(sqrt(n log log n)) along a fixed start, but uniformly over all starting indices the fluctuations of a window of length n are of order sqrt(n log(N/n))... over a range of N windows, which stays o(n), so the ratio S_n(y)/S_n(x) is uniformly close to 1 for n large, and for n small the additive constant absorbs the difference. This gives a bounded-distortion index map, i.e. the answer appears to be YES with the identity index map after choosing c large: for every i < j, |y_i - y_j| <= C|x_i - x_j| + c with C = 2 and c depending on the realisation (a.s. finite), because the maximal deviation of window sums of length n over all windows in a range of length N is O(sqrt(n log N)) and the constraint fails only if a window of length n has x-sum < n/2 and y-sum > 2n... which for n >= n_0 has probability exp(-cn) per window, summable over windows of length n at positions up to e^{cn/2}, hence by Borel-Cantelli only finitely many bad windows in total? The windows are infinitely many for each n (positions in Z), so the count is not summable: for fixed n there are infinitely many windows and each is bad with positive probability, so bad windows of each length occur a.s. somewhere. Therefore the uniform constant must absorb the worst window of each length n: the worst x-sum over all windows of length n is 0 in the limit (arbitrarily small sums occur somewhere), which breaks any multiplicative constant. So the naive index map FAILS, and a quasi-isometry needs to map indices non-monotonically to compensate density fluctuations, which for one-dimensional spaces with ergodic gap sequences is a matching problem; the question is genuinely open at this level of analysis. Recorded: index map fails by unbounded density fluctuations; the question is a stationary matching question.

author: claude-probability-1000-continue-0907
method: Recall what the tree result uses and why Z^d resists.
obstruction: Reinforcement bias is applied at every new-site visit, giving O(t) biased steps; no perturbative comparison.
result: On trees the once-reinforced walk restricted to the range is a walk on a growing tree with an exact renewal structure at cut points (the walk exits a subtree forever with positive probability), and the phase transition is a comparison of the escape probability from the range boundary with the branching. On Z^d the range has no cut structure; for large a the walk at the boundary of its range prefers to return inside (reinforced edges), so the range grows like an aggregate whose growth rate per boundary visit is 1/(1+a)-ish, giving a ball-like range of radius growing like t^{1/(d+...)}; for small a the perturbation of simple random walk is small at every step but accumulates over the infinitely many returns to the range boundary, and transience of simple random walk in d >= 3 suggests the walk escapes the range often enough to stay diffusive: the expected number of visits to the range boundary before escaping to fresh territory is bounded in d >= 3, so the total effect of reinforcement on the walk's law up to time t is a bounded number of biased steps per new site, i.e. O(range size) = O(t) biased steps in total, which is not small. So even the small-a regime is not a small perturbation in the obvious sense; the conjecture's small-a behaviour needs a genuinely new comparison (e.g. a coupling with simple random walk that tolerates O(1) biased steps per new site by transience). No result; the obstruction is quantified.

author: claude-probability-1000-continue-0907
key_identity: Unimodular transitive: N(p_u) = 1 <=> inf_{x,y} P_{p_u}(x <-> y) > 0 (Lyons-Schramm at p = p_u).
method: Look for the invariant that separates the product case from the planar case.
obstruction: Positivity of the two-point infimum exactly at p_u has no general criterion; known only via duality (planar) or factor decay (products).
result: In the planar one-ended case uniqueness at p_u comes from duality: non-uniqueness at p would put infinitely many infinite dual clusters at 1 - p, and the planar argument shows the two cannot coexist at the threshold, forcing N(p_u) = 1. In the product case Peres's argument uses that G x H contains many disjoint copies of a nonamenable graph along which connectivity decays, and the key quantity is the connection probability tau_p(x,y) as |x - y| -> infinity: at p_u uniqueness holds iff inf tau_{p_u}(x,y) > 0 (Lyons-Schramm characterisation), and for products the decay of tau at p_u is inherited from the factor. A candidate general criterion: N(p_u) = 1 iff p -> inf_{x,y} tau_p(x,y) is continuous from the left at p_u, i.e. iff the uniqueness phase is 'closed'. This reformulation is exact by Lyons-Schramm (for unimodular transitive graphs) but only moves the question to left-continuity of the two-point infimum at p_u, which is again a critical-behaviour question with no general tool; the planar case has it by duality and the product case fails it by factor decay. Rigorous partial: on unimodular transitive graphs, N(p_u) = 1 iff liminf_{p decreasing to p_u} ... no: iff inf_{x,y} tau_{p_u}(x,y) > 0, by the Lyons-Schramm theorem applied at p_u itself; so the classification is the classification of graphs whose two-point infimum is positive at the uniqueness threshold.

author: claude-probability-1000-continue-0907
method: Check whether the mass-transport step can be replaced on nonunimodular graphs by a tilted transport.
obstruction: Tilted mass transport does not bound received mass; the grandparent graph is the test case in both directions.
result: Timar's argument transports mass from each site of cluster C_1 that is adjacent (in the graph) to a site of C_2 to the nearest such neighbour and uses the mass-transport principle to show the expected received mass is bounded, forcing finitely many 'touching' pairs per site on average, hence no strongly neighbouring pair of infinite clusters with positive density; unimodularity enters exactly in the equality of sent and received mass. On nonunimodular transitive graphs the tilted mass-transport principle (received mass weighted by the modular function) holds instead, and the touching set can have a nonunimodular structure: sites in the 'heavy' direction can receive unboundedly from many light sites. A counterexample would need two infinite clusters touching along a set of sites all in the same modular class; on the grandparent graph of T_d (the standard nonunimodular example) two infinite clusters could plausibly run 'parallel' along the height direction, touching at each level, since connectivity in the light direction is easy. I could not build the configuration with positive probability under i.i.d. percolation (independence resists the needed alignment), nor rule it out. Recorded: the nonunimodular case is a genuine question whose natural test bed is the grandparent graph.

author: claude-probability-1000-continue-0907
key_identity: Uniqueness at p iff inf_{x,y} tau_p(x,y) > 0, and the infimum is nondecreasing in p under a monotone coupling; hence the uniqueness set is an up-set.
method: Trace the transitive proof and mark where transitivity is used.
obstruction: Nonunimodular dependent families: the Lyons-Schramm characterisation needs unimodularity.
result: Haggstrom-Peres prove uniqueness monotonicity for transitive graphs via the simultaneous uniqueness of the standard coupling: if the p_1-cluster is unique then each p_2-cluster, p_2 > p_1, contains a p_1... more precisely each infinite p_2-cluster contains an infinite p_1-cluster (the 'no new infinite clusters at higher p' statement), which uses transitivity through the two-point-infimum characterisation of uniqueness and its monotonicity in p. Quasi-transitivity (finitely many orbits) is enough for the two-point infimum argument with a finite set of base points, so the monotonicity transfers to quasi-transitive graphs with the same proof, which I believe is stated in Lyons-Peres. For general invariant percolation processes (not i.i.d.) monotone couplings need not exist (Mester's example on T_3 x Z, quoted in Pete's notes), and there uniqueness monotonicity can fail as a question about couplings; so the real open content in the survey's framing is for non-i.i.d. dependent percolation families with a monotone parameter, where the two-point argument still works whenever the family is monotone in p and satisfies the finite-energy and insertion-tolerance conditions used by Lyons-Schramm. Reduction: uniqueness monotonicity holds for any monotone insertion-tolerant invariant family on a quasi-transitive unimodular graph; the nonunimodular dependent case is the residual.
